citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $n\geq1$. Regarded as real Lie groups,

$$U(n)=\{A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C):A^*A=I\},\qquad SU(n)=\{A\in U(n):\det A=1\}$$

have Lie algebras

$$\mathfrak u(n)=\{X:X^*+X=0\},\qquad \mathfrak{su}(n)=\{X\in\mathfrak u(n):\operatorname{tr}X=0\}.$$

A **finite-dimensional real Lie group** is a group $G$, in the sense of
[[def-group]], together with the structure of a finite-dimensional real smooth
manifold such that the maps

$$m:G\times G\longrightarrow G,\qquad m(g,h)=gh,$$

and

$$\operatorname{inv}:G\longrightarrow G,\qquad \operatorname{inv}(g)=g^{-1},$$

are smooth in the sense of
[[def-smooth-map-between-manifolds-with-boundary]]. Its identity element is
denoted by $e$ (or occasionally $1$).

Unless an item explicitly says otherwise, every Lie group on this page is real,
finite-dimensional, and has no manifold boundary. Dimension zero is allowed;
for example, any countable discrete group with its discrete zero-dimensional
smooth structure is a Lie group. A Lie group cannot be empty because a group
contains its identity. The definition applies unchanged in dimension one,
uses no metric or nondegeneracy hypothesis, and makes no choice from a family
of sets.

derivations.claim: If $U,V\in SU(2)$, then $(UV)^*(UV)=V^*U^*UV=I_2$ and $\det(UV)=\det U\det V=1$. The identity belongs to $SU(2)$, and $U^{-1}=U^*$ is unitary with determinant $\overline{\det U}=1$. Thus the set is a group. Its standard smooth Lie-group structure and smooth matrix inclusion into $U(2)$ are supplied by [F2] under the definition [F3]. The map $\rho_2$ is a group homomorphism because it is the matrix inclusion, and it is unitary because $U^*U=I_2$.

In real coordinates the equations $U^*U=I_2$ and $\det U=1$ are continuous equations, so $SU(2)$ is closed. Unitarity makes each column a unit vector, hence every real and imaginary entry lies in $[-1,1]$; the set is bounded in $\mathbb R^8$. Apply [F1] to conclude compactness. The inherited Euclidean metric makes this subspace Hausdorff: for distinct $U,V$, the open balls of radius $\|U-V\|/3$ are disjoint, since a point in both would give $\|U-V\|<2\|U-V\|/3$ by the triangle inequality.

The matrices $A=\begin{pmatrix}i&0\\0&-i\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ are unitary with determinant one, while $AB=\begin{pmatrix}0&i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\-i&0\end{pmatrix}$ differ. Therefore $SU(2)$ is non-Abelian.

For $V\in SU(2)$, write its first column as $(\alpha,\gamma)$. Its second unit column orthogonal to the first is $\lambda(-\overline{\gamma},\overline{\alpha})$ for $|\lambda|=1$; determinant one gives $\lambda(|\alpha|^2+|\gamma|^2)=\lambda=1$. Hence $V=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\-\overline{\beta}&\overline{\alpha}\end{pmatrix}$ with $|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1$, and $\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2V=\operatorname{Re}\alpha\in[-1,1]$. Also $\operatorname{Tr}_2(V^{-1})=\operatorname{Tr}_2(V^*)=\overline{\operatorname{Tr}_2V}=\operatorname{Tr}_2V$, while cyclicity gives $\operatorname{Tr}_2(gVg^{-1})=\operatorname{Tr}_2V$. Thus the normalized trace is real, bounded, conjugation invariant, and inverse invariant.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
Assume AC. Every compact Hausdorff group has a unique left Haar probability measure. It is right invariant and inversion invariant as well.

Assume the axiom of countable choice. Let

$$SU(2):=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_2,\ \det U=1\}$$

with matrix multiplication and the topology induced by the eight real and imaginary matrix-entry coordinates. Equip it with its standard real Lie-group structure as the special unitary matrix group. Then $SU(2)$ is a compact Hausdorff non-Abelian finite-dimensional real Lie group. Its defining representation is the map $\rho_2:SU(2)\to U(2)$, $\rho_2(V)=V$, acting on $\mathbb C^2$ with the standard Hermitian form $h(v,w)=v^*w$; it is a smooth unitary group homomorphism.

Every $V\in SU(2)$ has the form $V=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\-\overline{\beta}&\overline{\alpha}\end{pmatrix}$ with $|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1$; consequently $\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2V=\operatorname{Re}\alpha\in[-1,1]$.

Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Fix the compact noncommutative finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$, its Lie algebra $\mathfrak g=T_eG$, and a specified smooth finite-dimensional complex unitary representation $\rho:G\to U(W,h)$ on a Hermitian vector space $(W,h)$ supplied by a non-Abelian gauge datum. Thus the group multiplication and inversion are smooth, $G$ is compact in its manifold topology, and $\rho(g)$ preserves $h$ for every $g\in G$. No connection, principal bundle sector, action functional, or continuum theory is part of the lattice data below.

A **finite oriented lattice two-complex** is a finite set $\mathcal V$ of vertices, a finite set $\mathcal E^+$ containing one chosen orientation of each edge, an endpoint map $s,t:\mathcal E^+\to\mathcal V$, and a finite set $\mathcal F$ of faces. Each face $p\in\mathcal F$ is supplied with a based closed edge word $(e_1,\ldots,e_k)$ in the oriented edges $\mathcal E^+\sqcup\overline{\mathcal E^+}$, where the endpoint of each edge is the starting point of the next and the last endpoint is the first starting point. For the reverse orientation $\bar e$ of $e\in\mathcal E^+$, set $s(\bar e)=t(e)$ and $t(\bar e)=s(e)$.

A **link configuration** is a tuple $U=(U_e)_{e\in\mathcal E^+}\in G^{\mathcal E^+}$, with $U_{\bar e}:=U_e^{-1}$. The **holonomy of a face** $p=(e_1,\ldots,e_k)$ is the ordered product $U_p:=U_{e_1}\cdots U_{e_k}$ in traversal order, with the first traversed edge on the left. The vertex gauge group is $G^{\mathcal V}$ with coordinatewise multiplication; write $\mathbf e=(e)_{v\in\mathcal V}$ for its identity tuple. It acts by

$$
(h\cdot U)_e=h_{s(e)}U_eh_{t(e)}^{-1},\qquad h=(h_v)_{v\in\mathcal V}\in G^{\mathcal V}.
$$

Choose a normalized bi-invariant Borel probability measure $\mu_G$ on $G$. The link measure is the finite product $\mu_G^{\mathcal E^+}$. For each face choose a continuous function $\Phi_p:G\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $\Phi_p(gzg^{-1})=\Phi_p(z)$ and $\Phi_p(z^{-1})=\Phi_p(z)$. Define the dimensionless lattice action and its normalized expectation by

$$
S_\Lambda(U):=\sum_{p\in\mathcal F}\Phi_p(U_p),\qquad Z_\Lambda:=\int_{G^{\mathcal E^+}}e^{-S_\Lambda(U)}\,d\mu_G^{\mathcal E^+}(U),\qquad \langle O\rangle_\Lambda:=Z_\Lambda^{-1}\int_{G^{\mathcal E^+}}O(U)e^{-S_\Lambda(U)}\,d\mu_G^{\mathcal E^+}(U)
$$

for bounded measurable $O:G^{\mathcal E^+}\to\mathbb C$. The finite-volume **Gauss sector** is the closed subspace of $L^2(G^{\mathcal E^+},\mathbb P_\Lambda)$ consisting of measurable functions with finite integral of $|f|^2$, modulo equality $\mathbb P_\Lambda$-almost everywhere, whose equivalence classes are invariant under each element of $G^{\mathcal V}$. Here $\mathbb P_\Lambda$ is the normalized probability with density $Z_\Lambda^{-1}e^{-S_\Lambda}$ relative to product link measure. For $v\in\mathcal V$ and $X\in\mathfrak g$, let $X^{(v)}$ be the tangent vector at the identity of $G^{\mathcal V}$ with component $X$ at $v$ and zero at other vertices. If $\alpha(h,U)=h\cdot U$, define the infinitesimal **Gauss generator** on $C^\infty(G^{\mathcal E^+})$ by

$$
(D_{v,X}f)(U):=df_U\!\left(d\alpha_{(\mathbf e,U)}(X^{(v)},0)\right).
$$

The full Gauss sector uses invariance under every vertex gauge transformation; the infinitesimal equations $D_{v,X}f=0$ alone are not asserted to impose invariance under disconnected components of $G$. Link variables and the action are dimensionless. This finite mathematical regulator makes no continuum-limit or empirical claim.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   The product measure of two sigma-finite measure spaces is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

On every measure space the pairing $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$ on complex $L^2$ is representative-independent, linear in the first variable, conjugate-linear in the second, conjugate symmetric and positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$. Moreover,
$$|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$
If $g\ne0$ as a class, equality holds iff $f=cg$ a.e. for some $c\in\mathbb C$. If $g=0$, equality holds for every $f$.

For each finite $m\ge0$, the same conclusions hold on tuples $F=(f_j)_{j<m}$, with pairing $B(F,G)=\sum_{j<m}\langle f_j,g_j\rangle$ and $\|F\|^2=\sum_{j<m}\|f_j\|_2^2$. For $G\ne0$, equality means $f_j=cg_j$ a.e. for every $j$, with one common scalar $c$.

derivations.claim: For $V\in SU(2)$, the parametrization in [F2] gives $\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2V\in[-1,1]$ and a real trace. Thus $\Phi(V)=\beta(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2V)$ is continuous. Cyclicity of trace gives $\operatorname{Tr}_2(gVg^{-1})=\operatorname{Tr}_2V$; unitarity gives $\operatorname{Tr}_2(V^{-1})=\overline{\operatorname{Tr}_2V}=\operatorname{Tr}_2V$. Hence each plaquette potential is conjugation- and inverse-invariant as required by [F3].

Each plaquette term therefore lies in $[0,2]$. Since $\mathcal P_\Lambda$ is finite, $0\leq S_\Lambda\leq2\beta|\mathcal P_\Lambda|$, and consequently $e^{-2\beta|\mathcal P_\Lambda|}\leq e^{-S_\Lambda}\leq1$.

The actions $S_s,S_t$ are sums of nonnegative plaquette terms by step 1.1, so $0\leq K(u',u)\leq1$. Matrix multiplication, inversion on $SU(2)$, and trace are continuous, so the temporal-action integrand is nonnegative and product-measurable. The slice and vertex product Haar measures are probabilities by [F1,F6], hence sigma-finite; Tonelli [F4] makes the $\eta$-integral $K$ measurable in $(u',u)$. Each slice Haar product is a probability by [F6], so $\int|K|^2\,d(\mu_s\times\mu_s)\leq1$.

The compact Hausdorff group in [F2] has its normalized Haar probability by [F1]. Apply the two-factor product-measure theorem [F6] successively along the finite ordered link set; the rectangle formula at each stage gives total mass one, and [F3] identifies this iterated product with $d\mu_\Lambda$. Integrating the bounds in step 2.1 gives $e^{-2\beta|\mathcal P_\Lambda|}\leq Z_\Lambda\leq1$. For bounded $O$, $\left|\int Oe^{-S_\Lambda}\,d\mu_\Lambda\right|\leq\|O\|_\infty Z_\Lambda<\infty$; division by the positive lower bound for $Z_\Lambda$ defines its normalized expectation.

Apply [F5] to $X_s=SU(2)^{E_s}$ with $\mathcal A_s=\bigotimes_{e\in E_s}\mathcal B(SU(2))$ and its original product probability $\mu_s$ from [F6]; [A1] supplies Countable Choice, so $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$ is a complex Hilbert space with the pairing in [F5]. Let $\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$ and choose a measurable representative. Since $d\mu_s$ is a probability, [F7] applied to $|\psi|$ and the constant function $1$ of norm one gives $\|\psi\|_{L^1(d\mu_s)}\leq\|\psi\|_{L^2(d\mu_s)}$. The kernel $K$ is measurable and satisfies $0\leq K\leq1$ by step 2.2, so $\int K(u',u)\psi(u)\,d\mu_s(u)$ converges absolutely for every $u'$ and is independent of the representative of $\psi$. The product function $(u',u)\mapsto K(u',u)\psi(u)$ is measurable, and its absolute integral over $d\mu_s(u')d\mu_s(u)$ is at most $\|\psi\|_{L^1(d\mu_s)}$; Tonelli [F4] applied to the positive and negative parts of its real and imaginary parts shows that the section integral $T\psi$ is measurable. For each $u'$, both $K(u',\cdot)^{1/2}$ and $K(u',\cdot)^{1/2}\psi$ lie in $L^2(d\mu_s)$, so [F7] applied to $K(u',\cdot)^{1/2}\psi$ and $K(u',\cdot)^{1/2}$ gives $|T\psi(u')|^2\leq\big(\int K(u',u)\,d\mu_s(u)\big)\big(\int K(u',u)|\psi(u)|^2\,d\mu_s(u)\big)\leq\int K(u',u)|\psi(u)|^2\,d\mu_s(u)$, because the first factor is at most one. Integrating in $u'$ and applying Tonelli again yields $\|T\psi\|_{L^2(d\mu_s)}^2\leq\int |\psi(u)|^2\big(\int K(u',u)\,d\mu_s(u')\big)d\mu_s(u)\leq\|\psi\|_{L^2(d\mu_s)}^2$, since $K\leq1$ and $d\mu_s$ is a probability. Linearity follows from linearity of the absolutely convergent section integral. Thus $T$ is a well-defined bounded linear operator with $\|T\|\leq1$.

Each spatial-link transformation is a left and right translation, so it preserves its Haar factor by [F1]; the rectangle formula and uniqueness in [F6] then show the product slice measure $d\mu_s$ is preserved. Under independent gauge transformations $h,h'$ of the incoming and outgoing slices, change temporal-link variables by $\eta_x\mapsto h_x\eta_x(h'_x)^{-1}$. Each such coordinate map also preserves Haar factors by [F1], and thus preserves $d\mu_V$ by [F6]. Substitution in $Q_{x,i}=\eta_xU'_{x,i}\eta_{x+\hat i}^{-1}U_{x,i}^{-1}$ cancels the neighboring $h'$ matrices and gives $Q_{x,i}\mapsto h_xQ_{x,i}h_x^{-1}$; each spatial plaquette is likewise conjugated at its base vertex. Trace invariance therefore preserves $S_t,S_s$, and the temporal integration gives $K(h'\cdot u',h\cdot u)=K(u',u)$ for every pair $(h',h)$. In particular, setting $h=1$ gives $K(h'\cdot u',u)=K(u',u)$. The pointwise integral definition established in step 3.2 now implies $(T\psi)(h'\cdot u')=(T\psi)(u')$ for every $u'$, hence as $L^2$ classes for each fixed $h'$, so $T\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$. The constant function has norm one because $d\mu_s$ is a probability and is fixed by every gauge transformation, so it is a nonzero physical vector.

Measure preservation from step 4.1 implies that pullback by $h^{-1}$ preserves measurable null sets, so $\mathcal U(h)$ is well-defined on almost-everywhere classes. It preserves the integral pairing from [F5] and has inverse $\mathcal U(h^{-1})$, hence is unitary on the complex Hilbert space established in step 3.2. Its fixed space is the kernel of the bounded operator $\mathcal U(h)-I$, hence is closed; the intersection over all $h$ is $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$, so $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ is closed.

In the cyclic product of kernels, each time slice contributes one half of $S_s(u_t)$ from the incoming factor and one half from the outgoing factor, summing to the full spatial action. Each temporal-link integral contributes exactly $e^{-S_t(u_{t+1},u_t;\eta_t)}$. Therefore the product integrand before temporal-link integration is the full $e^{-S_\Lambda}$; finite-product Tonelli [F4] gives the cyclic-kernel integral $Z_\Lambda$. For a bounded slice observable $O(u_0)$, the absolute value of its inserted integrand is bounded by $\|O\|_\infty e^{-S_\Lambda}\leq\|O\|_\infty$ on the finite product probability space [F6], so it is integrable. Applying [F4] to the positive and negative parts of its real and imaginary components justifies exchanging the integrations; the result is the corresponding unnormalized finite-volume expectation.

citations.quote:
Adopt the following pure-gauge Euclidean regulator. Assume full AC for normalized Haar-probability existence and for the L² transfer-operator framework. Let $N_s,N_t\geq3$ be integers, $a>0$ a common lattice spacing, and $g_0>0$ a dimensionless bare coupling. Use natural units $\hbar=c=1$. The finite periodic lattice is

$$\Lambda=(\mathbb Z/N_s\mathbb Z)^3\times(\mathbb Z/N_t\mathbb Z),$$

with spatial extent $L_s=N_sa$ in each spatial direction and Euclidean time extent $L_t=N_ta$. The global gauge group supplied by the finite non-Abelian lattice datum is

$$SU(2)=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_2,\ \det U=1\},$$

the compact Hausdorff non-Abelian Lie group established in the preceding local lemma, with its smooth defining two-dimensional unitary representation. Use that representation; $U^*$ denotes conjugate transpose and $\operatorname{Tr}_2$ its matrix trace. All link variables are dimensionless.

For each positive spatial direction $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, assign a link matrix $U_{x,i,t}\in SU(2)$ from $(x,t)$ to $(x+\hat i,t)$. Assign a temporal link matrix $\eta_{x,t}\in SU(2)$ from $(x,t)$ to $(x,t+1)$, with time understood modulo $N_t$. A reversed link carries the inverse matrix. Vertex gauge transformations are all functions $\Omega:\Lambda\to SU(2)$, acting by

$$U_{x,i,t}\mapsto \Omega_{x,t}U_{x,i,t}\Omega_{x+\hat i,t}^{-1},\qquad \eta_{x,t}\mapsto\Omega_{x,t}\eta_{x,t}\Omega_{x,t+1}^{-1}.$$

Let $E_\Lambda^+$ be the finite set of these positively oriented spatial and temporal links, let $\mathcal C_\Lambda:=SU(2)^{E_\Lambda^+}$ be the full link-configuration space with its finite-product topology, and equip it with the product Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B_\Lambda:=\bigotimes_{\ell\in E_\Lambda^+}\mathcal B(SU(2))$.

For $i<j$, define the spatial plaquette product

$$U_{x,ij,t}=U_{x,i,t}U_{x+\hat i,j,t}U_{x+\hat j,i,t}^{-1}U_{x,j,t}^{-1},$$

and define the temporal-spatial plaquette product

$$Q_{x,i,t}=\eta_{x,t}U_{x,i,t+1}\eta_{x+\hat i,t}^{-1}U_{x,i,t}^{-1}.$$

Set $\beta=4/g_0^2$, a positive dimensionless parameter. For a spatial slice $u=(U_{x,i})$, set

$$S_s(u)=\beta\sum_{x,\ i<j}\left(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2 U_{x,ij}\right),$$

and for adjacent slices $u',u$ and temporal links $\eta=(\eta_x)$, set

$$S_t(u',u;\eta)=\beta\sum_{x,\ i}\left(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2(\eta_xU'_{x,i}\eta_{x+\hat i}^{-1}U_{x,i}^{-1})\right).$$

The adopted Wilson action is $S_\Lambda=\sum_{t=0}^{N_t-1}\big(S_s(u_t)+S_t(u_{t+1},u_t;\eta_t)\big)$, with $u_{N_t}=u_0$. The compact Hausdorff group $SU(2)$ has the unique normalized left Haar probability measure $dU$, which is also right invariant under the assumed Axiom of Choice. On each positively oriented link use this measure; $d\mu_\Lambda$ is its finite product over the link set. For a bounded $\mathcal B_\Lambda$-measurable function $O:\mathcal C_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$, call $O$ gauge-invariant when $O(\Omega\cdot U)=O(U)$ for every vertex transformation $\Omega:\Lambda\to SU(2)$ and every $U\in\mathcal C_\Lambda$, where $\Omega\cdot U$ is the link configuration whose coordinates are the transformed links displayed above. The exact finite-volume partition function and the expectation of each such observable are

$$Z_\Lambda=\int e^{-S_\Lambda}\,d\mu_\Lambda,\qquad \langle O\rangle_\Lambda=Z_\Lambda^{-1}\int Oe^{-S_\Lambda}\,d\mu_\Lambda.$$

If $O$ represents a physical observable with assigned units, $\langle O\rangle_\Lambda$ has those same units; this postulate assigns no unit to the generic mathematical function $O$.

For the transfer convention, let $V_s=(\mathbb Z/N_s\mathbb Z)^3$ be the finite vertex set of one slice and $E_s=V_s\times\{1,2,3\}$ its positive spatial-link set. Define $d\mu_s:=\bigotimes_{(x,i)\in E_s}dU$ on $SU(2)^{E_s}$, where each factor is the normalized Haar Borel probability; let $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}=L^2(SU(2)^{E_s},d\mu_s;\mathbb C)$ be the complex $L^2$ space. Define $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}=\{\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm kin}:\mathcal U(h)\psi=\psi\text{ for every }h\in SU(2)^{V_s}\}$, where $\mathcal U(h)\psi(u)=\psi(h^{-1}\!\cdot u)$ in $L^2$. The finite-lattice well-definedness result establishes that this fixed subspace is closed. It is the group-invariant finite-slice Gauss sector. For one transfer step let $\eta=(\eta_x)_{x\in V_s}\in SU(2)^{V_s}$ denote its temporal-link tuple, and define $d\mu_V:=\bigotimes_{x\in V_s}dU$ on those coordinates, with each factor the normalized Haar Borel probability $dU$. Thus $d\mu_V$ is the finite product probability over all temporal links in one time step. Define

$$K(u',u)=e^{-\frac12S_s(u')-\frac12S_s(u)}\int_{SU(2)^{V_s}}e^{-S_t(u',u;\eta)}\,d\mu_V(\eta),\qquad (T\psi)(u')=\int K(u',u)\psi(u)\,d\mu_s(u).$$

The finite Euclidean time direction is assembled by iterating this one-step transfer operator, with the periodic boundary identification stated above. This is a Euclidean transfer convention only: no self-adjoint or positive-spectrum claim for $T$, no Lorentzian Hamiltonian identification, and no continuum or infinite-volume limit are postulated. The model has no dynamical matter fields, so it makes no matter-screening, confinement, or string-breaking claim. The regulator is adopted, not derived from a continuum theory or empirical evidence.

The quantities $a,L_s,L_t$ have units of length; $g_0,\beta,U_{x,i,t},\eta_{x,t},S_\Lambda,Z_\Lambda$ are dimensionless in the stated natural-unit convention. No measured parameter is supplied.

Assume full AC and use the finite non-Abelian lattice-data interface with global group $SU(2)$ and its smooth defining unitary representation on standard $\mathbb C^2$. Let $N_s,N_t\geq3$ be finite integers and let $a>0$, $\beta>0$. Use the finite periodic Euclidean lattice $\Lambda=(\mathbb Z/N_s\mathbb Z)^3\times(\mathbb Z/N_t\mathbb Z)$, with its finite oriented two-complex of vertices, positive spatial edges $(x,i,t)$, temporal edges $(x,t)$, and oriented plaquette boundary words. On every positive edge put an independent matrix in the compact Hausdorff Lie group

$$SU(2)=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_2,\ \det U=1\},$$

and assign its inverse to reverse traversal. A vertex function $\Omega:\Lambda\to SU(2)$ acts on an oriented link $U_{vw}$ by $U_{vw}\mapsto\Omega_vU_{vw}\Omega_w^{-1}$. $$S_\Lambda(U)=\beta\sum_{p\in\mathcal P_\Lambda}\left(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2U_p\right).$$

Let $dU$ be the unique normalized left Haar Borel probability measure on $SU(2)$, which is also right invariant, and use it as the bi-invariant link measure in the finite lattice-data interface. Define

$$Z_\Lambda=\int e^{-S_\Lambda(U)}\,d\mu_\Lambda(U).$$

For every bounded Borel-measurable function $O:\mathcal C_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$, the integral $\int Oe^{-S_\Lambda}\,d\mu_\Lambda$ is finite; moreover $0<Z_\Lambda\leq1$, so its normalized expectation is defined.

For a spatial slice $u=(U_{x,i})$, define the spatial plaquette action $S_s(u)$ by restricting the displayed action to spatial plaquettes. For two adjacent slices $u',u$ and temporal links $\eta_x$, define $S_t(u',u;\eta)$ by summing the same plaquette term over $\eta_xU'_{x,i}\eta_{x+\hat i}^{-1}U_{x,i}^{-1}$. Define $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}=\{\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm kin}:\mathcal U(h)\psi=\psi\text{ for every }h\in SU(2)^{V_s}\}$.

$$K(u',u)=e^{-\frac12S_s(u')-\frac12S_s(u)}\int e^{-S_t(u',u;\eta)}\,d\mu_V(\eta),\qquad (T\psi)(u')=\int K(u',u)\psi(u)\,d\mu_s(u).$$

Then $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ is closed and contains the nonzero constant function. $T$ is a bounded operator on $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$ with $\|T\|\leq1$ and maps $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$ into $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$. The cyclic product of $N_t$ kernels integrates to $Z_\Lambda$; insertion of any bounded slice observable gives the corresponding finite-volume unnormalized expectation. No self-adjointness, positivity as a quadratic form, Hamiltonian limit, or continuum statement is asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
Assume AC. Every compact Hausdorff group has a unique left Haar probability measure. It is right invariant and inversion invariant as well.

Assume the axiom of countable choice. Let

$$SU(2):=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_2,\ \det U=1\}$$

with matrix multiplication and the topology induced by the eight real and imaginary matrix-entry coordinates. Equip it with its standard real Lie-group structure as the special unitary matrix group. Then $SU(2)$ is a compact Hausdorff non-Abelian finite-dimensional real Lie group. Its defining representation is the map $\rho_2:SU(2)\to U(2)$, $\rho_2(V)=V$, acting on $\mathbb C^2$ with the standard Hermitian form $h(v,w)=v^*w$; it is a smooth unitary group homomorphism.

Every $V\in SU(2)$ has the form $V=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\-\overline{\beta}&\overline{\alpha}\end{pmatrix}$ with $|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1$; consequently $\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2V=\operatorname{Re}\alpha\in[-1,1]$.

Each action term is $\beta(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2 I_2)=0$, so $S_\Lambda=0$; the ordered product around $C$ is $I_2$, hence $W_C=1$. This evaluates the observable on one configuration only, not its probability or expectation.

The coordinate projection $U\mapsto u_0(U)$ is continuous for the finite-product topology, and matrix multiplication, inversion, and trace are continuous; hence $W_C:\mathcal C_\Lambda\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and Borel-measurable for the stated product Borel sigma-algebra. For a closed path $C=(x_0,\ell_1,x_1,\ldots,\ell_m,x_m)$ with $x_m=x_0$, each oriented factor transforms by the gauge matrix at its start and the inverse gauge matrix at its end. Adjacent factors cancel, leaving $U_C\mapsto\Omega_{x_0}U_C\Omega_{x_0}^{-1}$; cyclicity of trace proves gauge invariance. By [F3], for $V\in SU(2)$ one has $\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2V=\operatorname{Re}\alpha\in[-1,1]$. Thus $W_C$ is bounded by one in absolute value.

The choices $N_s=N_t=3$, $a>0$, and $g_0>0$ satisfy the finite-lattice hypotheses of [F1]. Applying [F1] gives a finite positive partition function, a defined normalized expectation for this bounded $W_C$, a bounded transfer operator preserving the Gauss sector, and a nonzero constant vector in that sector.

The same application of [F1] gives that the cyclic product of the one-step kernels integrates to the full periodic Euclidean Wilson weight, and that inserting $W_C$ on the chosen slice yields its stated finite-volume expectation. This is a fixed-lattice calculation; it contains no continuum or Lorentzian spectral assertion.
